points.en: Confidentiality is a stewardship serving the good of souls and the flock's protection, not an absolute wall behind which evil hides.
The governing principle: the seal of confidence yields when keeping it would leave someone in danger of serious harm.
It is a sacred trust, built slowly and shattered instantly, and the pastor should settle the limits before a crisis.
If someone intends to harm himself or another, the duty to protect life overrides secrecy; the pastor must get immediate real help, not merely pray.
If a child or vulnerable person is being abused, he must bring it to light and involve the authorities and protective help.
Silence is complicity, not discretion: a shepherd who shields a wolf to keep a confidence betrays the sheep.
He should know his land's reporting laws and settle his conscience before the crisis.
The pastor holds real power and intimate access to vulnerable people, so there is an imbalance of power between him and those under his care.
Therefore such a relationship is never mutual or between equals, and calling it mutual is a self-deceiving lie; it is abuse of the office's trust.
The greater guilt is the pastor's because the greater share of the power was his.
Fences: do not counsel the opposite sex alone behind closed doors; meet where visible, involve his wife or a mature woman, and keep door and schedule open.
Transparency protects because sin thrives in secrecy and withers in the light; an open life makes integrity easier to keep.
Such fences are ordinary prudence for a man whose heart is deceitful, not a sign of a dirty mind.
Not every transfer of membership is sheep-stealing; people relocate or leave for sincere reasons, and receiving a believer who comes in good order is not poaching.
The sin lies in the heart that recruits: targeting another congregation, courting its people or fanning their dissatisfaction to enlarge one's own.
It treats the kingdom as a competition between brothers with his congregation as the prize.
Philippians 2:3 forbids selfish ambition and conceit and calls us to esteem others better than ourselves.
Ephesians 4:3 calls us to keep the unity of the Spirit in peace, so building up by tearing down a brother's church gains members but loses unity.
Such ministry shows its true engine is ambition for one's own corner, not love for Christ's whole church.
The test: does he rejoice when a faithful church across town flourishes, even more than his own, or does its growth sour something in him?
Failing it reveals ambition and a failure to see that the kingdom is one and the sheep are Christ's, not his.
A written code forces a man to decide in the calm, before pressures arrive, what he will do in the storm.
Decisions should not be made in the heat of the moment when desire and self-interest cloud judgment; the code adds no rules to grace but gives settled convictions.
Examples: how to handle a confidence, a counseling boundary, or a neighboring church's member.
Honest references: telling the truth about a departing man, neither flattering him nor quietly destroying him with hints.
Honoring his predecessor rather than running him down, and serving his successor by leaving well.
Keeping his word, since a minister's promise once given is as good as a bond.
Handling church money and his own pay with transparency that invites scrutiny.
Colossians 4:5: walk in wisdom toward outsiders, because unbelievers read the pastor's conduct, and one act of dishonesty harms the gospel more than sermons can repair.
The ultimate purpose of the boundaries is a clean life, trustworthy word and open dealings that give the gospel a platform to be heard.
